questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: In my choice of University of Washington  (UW) academic opportunities were the most important thing. There was a highly esteemed Department of Communication at UW which intrigued me a lot as I sat at home and researched among different universities.  But the beautiful and vibrant surroundings of Seattle and Washington State was also an essential contributing factor to the final choice.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I has been the most wonderful experience full of tackled challanges and personal growth. The only reson i dot credit this bullet with the highest mark is due to the turbulent application process and the many misunderstandings between me, KU and UW.  Also, there were Covid restrictions in Washington at the beginning of 2022 which restricted the first two months of my stay a lot.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Very easy. UW is a large university and they are very used to having international students. UW Study Abroad, FUITS and ISS were organizations that helped out a lot in the beginning.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: FIUTS (Foundation for International Understanding Through Students)  was a great help. The did an emboark-session on Zoom within the first 1-2 weeks.  Also, we received several emails from Study Abroad in the first few weeks with important information regarding our visa status, special opportunities as international students etc.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: I think they did their job to perfection, honestly. It all seemed very professional and they always replied fast when one had questions or inquiries.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: It was decently easy. My advice would be to rent an airbnb the first few weeks, so that you can go sublease-hunting in person when you arrive. There is a plethora of Facebook groups where different offers are shared every day and often you can find cheaper opportunities than on-campus housing, if you are willing to live in a house or apartment with several roomies.  Don't expect Seattle to be cheaper than Copenhagen though. Because it is not.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: It is 100 pct. worth it! Try to look at neighborhoods such as Ravenna, U-Village, Green Lake or maybe even Capitol Hill if you like a more urban setting.  My advice would also be to look for a furnished sublease, as I ended up using quite a lot of money on the most basic furniture in my room (mattress, small desk, chair sheets and duvet etc.).

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It is decent but Seattle tends to be on the expensive side compared to Copenhagen. It is easy to find a place to live, but one cannot expect to live with a lot of privacy cheaply. One has to be willing to pay around 1500 USD for a studio appartment if one wants to live alone. For me, a subleased room in a house with several roommates was a good solution.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: There was a lot of misunderstandings and complications with me registering as an international graduate student at University of Washington, Seattle, which in the end costed me a lot of frustration, time and money.  In the end I had to apply as an undergraduate student to be accepted and enrolled, which was less than ideal. Honestly, though, I think the fault was more at poor information I received from UCPH Abroad which in the end caused me to miss deadlines. The hos institution, UW Study Abroad was actually pretty reliant in the registration process.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: UW Study Abroad gave us an email address where many of us exchange students had success getting help.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Once I was finally accepted, registration for classes was fairly decent. Because I wanted to take graduate courses but was enrolled in their system as an undergraduate, I had to communicate back and forth with all the professors to explain that I was academically skilled enough to take the classes. Again, this would have been easier if my graduate application had worked out. But I got all the courses that I hoped for except for one.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Be willing to fight a bit for the classes you want. Often a few emails to the right professors or a talk after class can get you far. The professors tend to reward academic interest as well as persistence.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
my impression was that there were plenty of relevant classes to choose from. Each class differ a lot from the other and it is my impression that the professors have more independence in how to structure curriculum and tests than in DK.  
Regarding level: If you choose 400 and 500-point classes, you can get them merited as MA classes. 300 and below are merited as BA classes.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: As said above, the professors at UW had more freedom was my impression. I had five different classes in 2 quarters and each was unique. They grade differently though. They accumulate grades the same way we do in DK in High school. Attendance, discussions, presentations and final exams accumulate your grade in the of the quarter on the 4.0 GPA scale.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Rhetoric of Science (5 credits)
Literature and Science (5 credits) 
Rhetorical Field Methods (5 credits)
Class, Labor and American Capitalism (5 credits) 
Contemporary American Public Address (5 credits)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Class, Labor and American Capitalism (5 credits) was a beautiful course for me, even though it was not within my original department (Communication).  I would recommend diving into any kind of classes which would give you background knowledge of the American culture, in which you find yourself at your exchange.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Seattle was just in general very expensive. Compared to my original budget food prices went through the roof in 2022. Especially if you also want to visit local restaurants, food markets etc.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Food! Concerts! Going out! Almost everything, honestly, were more expensive than expected - maybe also due to the sudden inflation in the US in the beginning of 2022. Transport was all right since you can bye a U-pass through the university which gives you total access to all public transport in Seattle (including several ferries!).

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Everything. I did mostly climbing, yoga and tennis but there were a plethora of social, cultural and sports opportunities.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: The organization FIUTS is a good way to meet other exchange students. Also, often the independent Scan Design Foundation will have some cool free events for Danish exchange students.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Try to see some of the nature outside of Seattle. If you team up with locals with a car (or rent one) Mount Ranier, Olympic and North Cascades national park are only a few hours away. If you come in the winter/fall then I would recommend all the ski opportunities, eg Crystal Mountain, which was frequently frequented by my roommates.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: It was fine, but of course, one has to be prepared that adjusting and adapting takes time - and it does not happen if you do not actively engage.  I would say it took me three months to feel at home in Seattle.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Meetup was an app I used to schedule hikes and events with local people from Seattle. It is a good way to meet people outside of the university environment.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: The US is not too bad. But the language barrier of course was difficult in the beginning.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Their relationship with nature. Everyone I met was pretty outdoorsy and was always on their way to summit some mountain or on their way skiing. A wonderful way to live.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: Team up with other exchange students from KU beforehand. The application process at KU is ridiculous and you risk being faulty advised, but it is all easier if you help each other out. Be persistent in communicating with home and host universities. As soon as you are in the States, everything will work itself out. :-)

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Be prepared to study a lot too as UW require you to "overload" compared to what you will be merited for by KU. I had 25 credits completing five classes, which in total which equals 50 ECTS. Though, I will only be merited for 30 ECTS from KU (three of the classes). The Winter quarter starts in early January.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Meeting new people.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Getting there in the first place. The application process took a lot of (unnecessary) effort.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
